title: Design a Notification System
subtitle: Send one event out as push, email, and SMS, and watch preferences, dedup, queues, retries, and rate limits keep it safe.
learn: Why notifications are sent through per-channel queues instead of directly from the caller
How a preference service and quiet hours decide who gets what, before anything is queued
How idempotency keys stop duplicate sends, and why delivery is at-least-once
How retries with backoff, dead-letter queues, and rate limits survive flaky providers
How to size the system from daily volume to peak sends per second

steps.title: One event, three channels
steps.body: A user's order ships. The shipping service wants to tell them: a push notification to their phone, an email with the tracking link, maybe an SMS. Assume 10 million users and about 50 million notifications a day, which is roughly 600 a second on average and about 10 times that in a burst. How do you deliver all of it once, on the right channel, without overloading a provider or spamming anyone?
steps.idea: A notification system is a pipeline that decides whether, where, and when to send, then sends reliably.
steps.caption: An upstream service has something to tell a user.

steps.title: Accept fast, send later
steps.body: The shipping service calls the Notification API with an event: a user id, a template, and some data. The API validates it, runs the checks in the next steps (preferences and duplicates), saves the messages safely in queues (waiting lines for messages), and only then answers 202 Accepted, meaning "received, not yet sent". This takes tens of milliseconds. The API never waits for the provider, because sending is slow and flaky (100 ms to several seconds) and must not hold up the caller.
steps.idea: Decouple the caller from delivery: acknowledge once the event is durably stored, never after the slow send.
steps.caption: The event reaches the API, which validates it before doing anything else.

steps.title: Ask the preference service
steps.body: Before queuing anything, the API asks the preference service what this user wants. Is push allowed for shipping updates? Did she unsubscribe from email? Is it 3 a.m. in her time zone? If so, non-urgent sends go to a delay queue until quiet hours end. Opt-outs and legal consent live here too. Checking first avoids queuing what we may not send. For marketing messages, workers re-check the opt-out flag just before sending, so an unsubscribe or an SMS "STOP" takes effect at once.
steps.idea: Preferences are a gate in front of the queues: opt-outs, channel choice, and quiet hours are decided before any work is queued.
steps.caption: The preference service answers: push and email yes, SMS no.

steps.title: Dedup with an idempotency key
steps.body: Upstream services retry, and message brokers redeliver, so the same event can arrive twice. To catch repeats, the API builds a key from user, template and event id, then runs one atomic Redis command, SET ... NX (set only if the key does not exist). It stores "in progress" with a short expiry. Once the message is queued, the key becomes "done" for 24 hours. A retry that finds "done" is dropped. If the API crashed midway, the short expiry lapses and the retry resumes. Without this, one retried order event means two emails.
steps.idea: A two-state idempotency key makes a repeated request harmless without ever losing the first one.
steps.caption: The key has not been seen before, so the event continues.

steps.title: One queue per channel
steps.body: The API renders a small message for each allowed channel and puts it on that channel's own queue: push and email here. Once they are safely queued, it marks the dedup key done and answers the caller with 202 Accepted. Separate queues matter because channels behave differently: push is fast and bulk, email is slower, and SMS is costly and tightly limited. If the SMS provider stalls, only its queue grows while push and email keep flowing.
steps.idea: Per-channel queues isolate failures and let each channel scale and throttle on its own.
steps.caption: Messages split into one queue per channel, then the caller gets its 202.

steps.title: Workers send, within limits
steps.body: Channel workers take messages from a queue and call the provider: APNs and FCM (Apple's and Google's push services), an email service, or an SMS gateway. Before each call, a worker takes a token from a token bucket in Redis. The bucket refills at a steady rate and each send spends one token. If it is empty, the worker waits. This keeps us under provider limits and SMS costs. Per-user caps (for example 3 marketing pushes a day) stop one person being flooded. The provider then replies that it accepted the message.
steps.idea: Rate limits protect the provider relationship, the budget, and each user; workers pull at the speed the limits allow.
steps.caption: Workers take a token to stay within limits, then call the provider.

steps.title: The provider fails
steps.body: Now the email provider returns 503 errors. Only temporary errors are retried (5xx, 429 with Retry-After, timeouts); permanent 4xx errors like a bad address are not. The worker puts the message back on the queue with a delay that doubles from 1 s up to about 5 minutes, plus random jitter so thousands of retries do not arrive at once. A circuit breaker pauses workers while the provider is down. Messages expire by type: an OTP (one-time code) is stale in minutes, a shipping notice can wait hours. Past expiry or the attempt cap, a message goes to a dead-letter queue, a holding area to replay after recovery, so nothing is silently lost.
steps.idea: Retry transient errors with capped backoff and jitter, expire stale messages, and park the rest in a dead-letter queue.
steps.caption: Failed sends go back on the queue with a growing delay.

steps.title: At-least-once means duplicates
steps.body: A worker sends the email, then crashes before telling the queue it finished. The queue redelivers the message, so a second email could go out. Exactly-once delivery over a network is not achievable here, so we choose at-least-once and shrink duplicates. Before sending, the worker marks the notification id "sending" in Redis with a short lease, and "sent" once the provider accepts. A redelivery that finds "sent" skips. One that finds only an expired "sending" tries again, using the provider's idempotency key if it has one. A rare duplicate beats a lost message.
steps.idea: Pick at-least-once delivery and make sending idempotent; a rare duplicate beats a lost notification.
steps.caption: The redelivered message finds "sent" in Redis and is skipped.

steps.title: A flash sale spike
steps.body: Marketing launches a promo to 5 million users. A campaign job turns it into per-user events at a controlled rate, about 8,000 pushes per second against a 600 per second average. The queues absorb the burst, so the API stays fast. Workers drain the push queue at their rate limit, and you add workers when the oldest message gets too old. Priority matters too: password resets and payment alerts go on a high-priority queue, so a promo never delays them.
steps.idea: Queues turn a spike into a backlog; separate priorities keep urgent messages ahead of bulk ones.
steps.caption: A backlog builds in the queue, then drains at the allowed rate.

steps.title: The whole pipeline
steps.body: Accept the event fast, check preferences, dedup with an idempotency key, then queue per channel. Workers send within rate limits, retry with backoff, park failures in a dead-letter queue, and guard against duplicates at send time. Watch queue age, delivery rate and provider errors per channel to see which stage is hurting. Provider feedback (bounces, complaints, dead push tokens) flows back into preferences so bad addresses stop being targeted.
steps.idea: Gate, dedup, queue per channel, send within limits, retry safely: each stage removes one failure mode.
steps.caption: Each stage guards against one kind of failure.

quiz.q: Why does the Notification API return 202 Accepted and put messages on queues instead of calling the email provider directly?
options: Queues make emails arrive faster than direct calls
Provider calls are slow and flaky, so the caller should not wait on them, and a queue lets us buffer and retry
Providers refuse direct calls from application servers
It lets us skip the preference check
quiz.why: Sending is slow and can fail. A queue decouples the caller, absorbs bursts, and gives a place to retry. It does not make a single email faster.

quiz.q: The email provider has an outage for 10 minutes. Which design keeps push notifications flowing normally?
options: A single shared queue with FIFO order
Sending push and email in the same worker call
Retrying email immediately in a tight loop
One queue and worker pool per channel
quiz.why: Per-channel queues isolate failures: the email backlog grows while push workers keep draining their own queue.

quiz.q: A worker sends an email, then crashes before acknowledging the queue message. What does an at-least-once system do, and how do we limit the harm?
options: The message is lost; add more workers
It sends exactly once by design, so nothing is needed
It redelivers the message; a send marker keyed by notification id lets the next worker skip the duplicate
It moves the message to the dead-letter queue immediately
quiz.why: Queues redeliver unacknowledged messages. A two-state send marker (sending, then sent) lets the next worker skip a finished send, while an expired 'sending' is retried, favoring a rare duplicate over a loss.

quiz.q: Retries after a provider outage all fire at the same moment and knock the provider over again. What is the best fix?
options: Retry as fast as possible to finish sooner
Exponential backoff with random jitter and a maximum attempt count
Never retry; drop the messages
Retry every message exactly every 10 seconds
quiz.why: Backoff spreads load over time, jitter prevents synchronized retry waves, and a cap plus dead-letter queue stops endless retrying.

quiz.q: A marketing blast of 5 million messages is queued. Which step best protects password-reset notifications from long delays?
options: Use a separate high-priority queue that workers drain first
Give each user a bigger rate limit
Add more workers to the shared bulk queue only
Increase the retry count
quiz.why: Priority queues keep urgent, time-sensitive messages from waiting behind bulk traffic, even when the bulk backlog is large.

cheatsheet.def: A unique id for an event or send. Stored in two states (in progress, then done) with an expiry; a second request with a done key is ignored, and a crashed first attempt can resume.
Messages are redelivered until acknowledged, so none are lost but duplicates are possible. Handle duplicates with idempotent sends.
Wait longer after each failure (1s, 2s, 4s...) plus a random offset so many retries do not synchronize.
Holds messages that exceeded their retry cap, so they can be inspected or replayed instead of vanishing.
Rate limiter: tokens refill at a steady rate, each send takes one, and an empty bucket means wait. Allows small bursts.
A user setting that delays non-urgent notifications during certain local hours. Urgent types such as security alerts may bypass it.
Often a better alert signal than depth, because it shows user-visible delay.
50M a day is about 580 per second average; plan for 10x peaks and size workers from provider throughput and latency.

lab.prompt: Design the notification system for a marketplace with 20M users sending 100M notifications a day across push, email, and SMS. Sketch the components, data flow, and failure handling on paper.
requirements: Accept events from many internal services and respond in under 50 ms
Respect per-user channel preferences, opt-outs, and quiet hours
Never send the same notification twice in normal operation, even when callers retry
Survive a provider outage without losing messages
Deliver urgent notifications such as security codes within 10 seconds, even during a promo blast
Stay within each provider's rate limits and the SMS budget
hints: Compute average and peak sends per second first: 100M a day is about 1,160 per second, so plan for 10x or more at peak.
Put the preference check and idempotency check before queuing, so we avoid queuing work we cannot send.
Use one queue per channel, and a separate high-priority queue for urgent types.
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, cap attempts, and add a dead-letter queue.
Rate limit per provider, and consider per-user limits so one user is not flooded with ten messages in a minute.
Decide what happens if Redis is unavailable: fail open and risk duplicates, or fail closed and delay.
checklist: Is the caller decoupled from delivery by a queue, with preferences and opt-outs checked before anything is queued?
Do both an idempotency key at the API and a send marker at the worker exist?
Does each channel have its own queue and worker pool?
Are retries bounded, with backoff, jitter, and a dead-letter queue?
Is there a priority path for urgent notifications?
Do you monitor queue age, delivery rate, and provider error rate per channel?
Is there a fallback provider or channel when one provider is down?
